column13: As written: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome day of the Lord" (Malachi 3:23). In the third watch, spiritual awareness is felt exclusively by fully developed human beings; and because the light of day draws near, they are awakened through the supernal roar Above, which emerges directly out of sensing the approaching light.

column11: Temurah 16a: ‘The Gemara cites yet another verse involving Achsah: “And she said: Give me a blessing; for that you have set me in the land of the South [negev], and you have given me springs of water. column11: Bava Kamma 92a: ‘§ The Gemara cites a series of questions that Rava asked Rabba bar Mari, the first one being related to the previous topic of discussion. column13: And therefore they compared [there in Sanhedrin] [Israel] to “a myrtle standing among thorns [chilfei]” — for “the sins are only like the thorns surrounding the myrtle,” but “the essence of the myrtle is unchanged.” — the Jew’s sins are the surrounding thornbush — exile’s pressure and the “leaven in the dough” — while the fragrant myrtle at the center, his bond to God, is never so much as touched.

column11: Berakhot 35b: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai says: Is it possible that a person plows in the plowing season and sows in the sowing season and harvests in the harvest season and threshes in the threshing season and winnows in the windy season, as grain is separated from the chaff by means of the wind, and is constantly busy; what will become of Torah? Rather, one must dedicate himself exclusively to Torah at the expense of other endeavors; as when Israel performs God’s will, their work is performed by others, as it is stated: “And strangers will stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners will be your plowmen and your vinedressers” (Isaiah 61:5). column11: Sanhedrin 99b: ‘Rabbi Elazar says: Every man was created for labor, as it is stated: “Man is born for toil” (Job 5:7). Based on this verse, I do not know whether he was created for toil of the mouth, speech, or whether he was created for the toil of labor. When the verse states: “For his mouth presses upon him” (Proverbs 16:26), you must say that he was created for toil of the mouth. And still I do not know with regard to the toil of the mouth whether it is for the toil of Torah or for the toil of conversation. When the verse states: “This Torah scroll shall not depart from your mouth” (Joshua 1:8), you must say that he was created for the toil of Torah. And that is the meaning of what Rava said: All…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 3, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 99b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And as written (Sanhedrin 99b): ''When it says 'shall not depart, etc.'—say that he was created for the toil of Torah, etc., happy is he who merits to become the pack-bearer (wholly consumed) of...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For all human endeavors culminate in speech, as is written: "All the labor of man is for his mouth," and our Sages expounded (Sanhedrin 99b): "I do not know whether this means the labor of Torah or the labor of speech, etc."; the meaning being as written in the Zohar, Emor (105a): that there is not a single word uttered that does not ascend, etc., see there his full wording.

column11: Taanit 24b: ‘§ The Gemara continues to discuss the righteous Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa and the wonders he performed. column11: Chullin 84a: ‘“For your food, for the food of your household” indicates that your food comes before the food of your household, i.e., one must first ensure that he has food for himself before providing for others. From here, the Torah taught that it is a desired mode of behavior that a person should not accustom his son to eat meat and drink wine; rather, he should teach his children to eat less expensive foods.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 3, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chullin 84a) to illuminate his exposition here (“similar to what we find (Chullin 84a): 'And when for the rest? column15: Uses the term hitnasut, for a state of spiritual elevation. The sons of Kehat achieved this by deliberately entering themselves into situations of doubt and uncertainty, and by being tested. Of this it is said (Bamidbar, 7:9), “and he [Moses] did not give [wagons] to the sons of Kehat, upon them is a holy service, yisa’u - they shall carry upon the shoulder.” In other words, from yisas’u, the act of carrying on their shoulder, a cognate of nasso, or raise, we learn that they had reached the state of patience necessary to enter into and cope with places of uncertainty.

column11: Berakhot 35b: ‘The Sages taught: What is the meaning of that which the verse states: “And you shall gather your grain”? column13: And this section is articulated in the plural, which is why "with all your might" was omitted, that being the ultimate depth of the supernal Will as noted above. And with "and you shall gather" (ve-asafta) the text reverts to the singular, because within the collective plural are contained all categories of individuals, and for their totality "I will give, etc." applies, the influx descending unto all; and it is unique to one who enters and exits in the entrance and exit mentioned above, where the exit is likewise necessary for the entrance, seeing that one cannot remain in continuous cleaving at all times.

column11: Nazir 4a: ‘The Gemara asks: And according to the Rabbis also, isn’t the verse needed to prohibit to a nazirite wine that is consumed as a mitzva, just like wine whose consumption is optional? column11: Bava Batra 12b: ‘Having already cited one statement of Rabbi Avdimi from Haifa, the Gemara cites another statement in his name: Rabbi Avdimi from Haifa says: Before a person eats and drinks he has two hearts, meaning his heart is unsettled because he is distracted by hunger. And this flows from the side of Yitzchak, for "the Torah issued from the side of Gevurah" (Zohar III, 80b); within Yitzchak being the supreme revelation of the love of Torah which is the antithesis of lust.

column11: Yoma 71a: ‘The verse states: “To you men [ishim] do I call, and my voice is to the sons of men” (Proverbs 8:4). column11: Berakhot 5a: ‘And Rabbi Levi bar Ḥama said that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: God said to Moses, “Ascend to Me on the mountain and be there, and I will give you the stone tablets and the Torah and the mitzva that I have written that you may teach them” (Exodus 24:12), meaning that God revealed to Moses not only the Written Torah, but all of Torah, as it would be transmitted through the generations. column15: 12–17: Prior to the Flood, animals dwelled in pristine perfection, mating strictly after their kind, perceiving their root; wherefore Adam was forbidden to eat them, needing no human elevation, being whole in themselves. column15: 22–25: For in every soul an innate imperfection resides, as it is written (Psalms 51:7): “And in sin did my mother conceive me.” This stems from the primordial chaos (tohu) that preceded creation, and man through his divine labor possesses the power to rebuild that which is ruined and desolate. Likewise, all unruly, impulsive drives within man correspond to the “worlds that were shattered”; and through spiritual work man can channel these raw energies into holiness, and upon entering the realm of sanctity they become supremely precious.

column11: Shabbat 146a: ‘the snake came upon Eve, i.e., when it seduced her to eat from the Tree of Knowledge, it infected her with moral contamination, and this contamination remained in all human beings. Rav Aḥa, the son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi: What about converts? How do you explain the cessation of their moral contamination?
